title: Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access
clue: An FTP banner or accessible listing
conditions: Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: Retrieved files, configuration or a verified writable location
mechanics: FTP authentication and directory listing do not guarantee downloads or uploads. Passive/active data channels can fail independently of the control connection; uploaded bytes need a separate execution consumer.
example: Observation: anonymous login succeeds. Test: list and download one relevant readable configuration. Illustrative output: an application username is present. Interpretation: classify its credential context and test only a compatible service.
verify: Retrieve recognizable bytes or independently verify an uploaded canary; distinguish listing, read and write rights.
failure: Login succeeds but transfers hang: diagnose the data path. A writable upload directory alone does not establish command execution.

recognition.where: After identifying FTP, test the allowed anonymous context or one known credential and inspect its directory namespace.
recognition.sample:
230 Login successful
LIST: application.conf; backups/
RETR application.conf: 226 Transfer complete
recognition.spot: A listing identifies candidate artifacts; a completed RETR with recognizable bytes establishes read access.
recognition.confirm: Validate the account context, file contents, data-channel reachability and any separate write/consumer conditions.
recognition.enabled: The relevant file is readable and contains a current typed secret: follow credential classification.
recognition.ruledout: Anonymous login is denied: rule out anonymous access, retaining authenticated FTP as a separate possibility.
recognition.unknown: Login works but data transfer hangs: inspect active/passive data routing before concluding file access is denied.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** FTP usually appears on TCP/21, but trust an FTP banner or protocol response on any port. **Goal:** determine authentication, listable/readable content and effective write locations. ##### Baseline: anonymous access ```bash ftp TARGET ``` At the prompts, try user `anonymous` and an email-like password. Then: ```text status pwd ls -la binary get FILE quit ``` If login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's `passive` command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. > **Decisive output:** code `230` accepts the login; directory listings and successful `RETR` establish read access. Inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. Store target artifacts outside this public repository.
Variant — authenticated FTP ```bash ftp TARGET ``` Enter `USER` and the password when prompted. Enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access.
Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test ```bash curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER ftp://TARGET/ curl --user USER -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt ``` Omit `--user` for anonymous access. Let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. Upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the FTP client after the test.
Variant — focused Nmap helpers ```bash nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET ``` `ftp-anon` checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; `ftp-syst` asks for server/system information. Manually confirm useful access with a protocol client.
> **Failure cues:** `530` means that login was rejected, not that FTP has no other usable identity. A listing failure after `230` may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. A successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. > **Next action:** inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block.

title: Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access
clue: An SSH service and a known password, private key or agent context
conditions: Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: An authenticated shell, subsystem or forwarding capability with verified identity
mechanics: SSH authentication can succeed while shell access is restricted. Key ownership, passphrase and server authorization matter independently; forwarding is a separately controlled feature.
checks:
```bash
ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET
ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET
```
example: Observation: a disclosed private key names a local user. Test: inspect the key and authenticate to that user. Illustrative output: a shell returns with a non-root UID. Interpretation: establish Linux state and inspect allowed forwarding.
verify: Run hostname and id in the resulting context; retain whether a shell, SFTP or only forwarding was actually granted.
failure: Permission denied may be username, key, passphrase, policy or method mismatch. A successful banner exchange proves none of these.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** SSH commonly uses TCP/22. **Prerequisite for access:** an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. ##### Baseline: validate one known identity ```bash ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. A shell prompt establishes session access as that identity.
Variant — private key ```bash chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` The key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions.
Variant — discover methods for a known username ```bash nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET ``` This starts an authentication exchange and is logged; Nmap classifies it as intrusive. Use it only when the supported methods change the next decision.
Variant — non-interactive key check ```bash ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET 'id' ``` Batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. It is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively.
> **Failure cues:** timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; `Permission denied` proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. A valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. > **Next action:** after a shell, verify `whoami`, groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. Password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure.

title: Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols
clue: SMTP capabilities or mail-related account clues
conditions: Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: Validated mail capabilities, possible usernames or authenticated mailbox artifacts
mechanics: VRFY/RCPT differences may disclose account existence but catch-all policy can invalidate inference. A valid recipient is not an authenticated mailbox or operating-system login.
example: Observation: two recipient probes produce different replies. Test: compare known-invalid controls and repeated responses. Illustrative output: only one candidate is consistently accepted. Interpretation: retain a possible username and check account context before authentication testing.
verify: Record response/control differences and separate inferred account existence from successful mailbox authentication.
failure: Uniform replies, disabled VRFY or a catch-all make username enumeration inconclusive; investigate other identity sources.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** SMTP commonly uses TCP/25, submission uses 587, and implicit TLS commonly uses 465. **Goal:** collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. ##### Baseline: banner and capabilities ```bash nc -nv TARGET PORT ``` Then enter: ```text EHLO example.invalid HELP VRFY USER EXPN postmaster QUIT ``` > **Decisive output:** `250-` capability lines reveal extensions such as STARTTLS or AUTH. `250` after `VRFY` may support a valid mailbox; `550` commonly rejects or denies it; `252` explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists.
Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet ``` Run `EHLO example.invalid` after TLS negotiation. Certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism.
Variant — focused automated user checks ```bash smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT ``` `RCPT` testing requires an SMTP transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. Treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses.
Variant — Windows source position ```powershell Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORT ``` This verifies TCP reachability only. Use an available Netcat/Ncat or OpenSSL client for protocol dialogue.
> **Failure cues:** multiline replies begin with `NNN-` and finish with `NNN `; read the final line. `503` often means the command sequence is wrong. Uniform `252` or `550` responses make enumeration inconclusive. A visible AUTH method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. > **Next action:** add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. Do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. ##### POP3 and IMAP handoff Mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995 -crlf -quiet # POP3S openssl s_client -connect TARGET:993 -crlf -quiet # IMAPS ``` POP3 dialogue: ```text CAPA USER USER PASS PASSWORD STAT LIST QUIT ``` IMAP dialogue: ```text a1 CAPABILITY a2 LOGIN USER PASSWORD a3 LIST "" "*" a4 LOGOUT ``` > Test one legitimately acquired credential. Capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force NSE scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap mail blocks.

title: Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers
clue: A DNS server, domain name or host aliases
conditions: Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: Hostnames, address relationships and possibly a zone inventory
mechanics: A DNS answer belongs to a server and zone context. AXFR exposes zone records only when the server is authoritative and permits the transfer; names become discovery or virtual-host inputs.
checks:
```bash
dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA
dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS
dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR
```
example: Observation: the authoritative server permits AXFR. Test: inspect the returned A/CNAME records. Illustrative output: a previously unknown application hostname. Interpretation: confirm scope/address reachability and request that virtual host.
verify: Identify responding server, record type, answer and zone authority; transfer refusal disproves only that transfer/context.
failure: No answer may mean wrong server, recursion policy, transport or zone. Resolve authoritative context before retrying AXFR.

recognition.where: Use DNS-server evidence and discovered domain names to query authority and specific records before considering a transfer.
recognition.commands:
```bash
dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA
dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS
dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR
```

HOSTNAME.DOMAIN. A TARGET

recognition.spot: An authoritative zone and returned records can expose hostnames, aliases and applications needing separate enumeration.
recognition.confirm: Check each new name's scope/address and verify host/virtual-host behavior.
recognition.enabled: A permitted transfer returns a relevant new host: validate it through discovery.
recognition.ruledout: Transfer refused rules out AXFR on this server/zone/context; ordinary records may remain useful.
recognition.unknown: A timeout or non-authoritative response requires authority/transport checks before any zone conclusion.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries and TCP/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. **Prerequisite:** a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. ##### Baseline: query the target DNS server directly ```bash dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN A dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT ``` > **Decisive output:** `ANSWER` records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. The `aa` flag supports an authoritative answer. Record `status` separately from the answer count.
Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer ```bash dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR ``` A successful AXFR returns the zone records and closing SOA. `Transfer failed`, `REFUSED` or `NOTAUTH` only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries.
Variant — name guessing after the domain is known ```bash dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN ``` Check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. Every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input.
Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range ```bash dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET ``` Use this only when the entire `SUBNET` is assigned. PTR names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results.
Variant — host and Windows nslookup ```bash host -t mx DOMAIN TARGET host -t txt DOMAIN TARGET ``` ```powershell nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=MX DOMAIN TARGET ```
> **Failure cues:** `NXDOMAIN` means that queried name does not exist in that view; `NOERROR` with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. Timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. A recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. > **Next action:** add new hostnames/IPs to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** direct-hosted SMB commonly uses TCP/445; NetBIOS session service commonly uses TCP/139; MS-RPC endpoint mapping commonly uses TCP/135. They are related Windows surfaces but not interchangeable. **Goal:** distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. ##### Baseline: list shares without credentials ```bash smbclient -N -L //TARGET ``` > **Decisive output:** a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. It does not prove access to share contents. `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential.
Variant — authenticated share listing and connection ```bash smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' ``` The first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. Let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. Inside the share: ```text pwd ls allinfo FILE get FILE mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit ``` Use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. A successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution.
Variant — recursive retrieval ```bash smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON;prompt OFF;mget *' ``` Run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. Search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data.
Variant — RPC null or authenticated session ```bash rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET ``` Useful interactive queries: ```text srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser RID netshareenumall quit ``` Null-session denial is common on modern systems. Authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it.
Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates ```bash nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET ``` NetExec (`nxc`) is the current command name on recent Kali releases; older material may use `crackmapexec`. These tools consolidate candidates. Confirm useful shares and files with `smbclient` or native access.
Variant — protocol, signing and time clues ```bash nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET ``` Signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. The older `smb-os-discovery` script depends on SMBv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably.
Variant — Windows built-ins ```powershell net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE ``` These use the current Windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. An existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors.
> **Failure cues:** distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. A share named `IPC$` is not a general file share. Guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. A share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. > **Next action:** inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. Move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/AD blocks.

title: Extract configuration and process information through SNMP
clue: UDP/161 evidence or an exposed management plane
conditions: An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: Host, interface, software or process/configuration clues from permitted OID branches
mechanics: An SNMP community acts as an access selector; views can expose only some trees. A successful system OID does not grant write access or all process data.
example: Observation: a system OID responds. Test: inspect the relevant interface/process branch. Illustrative output: an internal subnet and application command line. Interpretation: return the subnet to scoped discovery and classify any exposed credential.
verify: Preserve the OID, accepted security context and returned value; empty branches can reflect view restrictions.
failure: Silence can mean UDP filtering, wrong community/version or denied view; change only the condition supported by evidence.

SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: HOSTNAME
recognition.spot: A real OID response confirms the accepted read context and supplies software/name clues.

procedure:
> **Recognize:** SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. **Goal:** turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. ##### Baseline: find a read community, then walk ```bash onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Use `-v1` instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. > **Decisive output:** returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path.
Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk ```bash snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to `snmpwalk` with the verified version.
Variant — high-value Windows OIDs ```bash snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 ``` These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view.
Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk ```bash snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 ``` The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. `authNoPriv` authenticates without encryption; `noAuthNoPriv` supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed.
Variant — focused UDP verification ```bash sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET ``` `snmp-info` extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community.
> **Failure cues:** UDP silence can remain `open|filtered`; it does not prove that the community is wrong. `Timeout: No Response` can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. `No Such Object` means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. > **Next action:** translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage.

clue: LDAP/Kerberos listeners or a probable AD domain
conditions: Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context
access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential
result: A directory base DN and permitted account/group/computer attributes
mechanics: RootDSE can disclose naming contexts without permitting subtree enumeration. A bind identity, search base and attribute/object ACLs independently constrain results.
example: Observation: RootDSE returns a base DN. Test: attempt the permitted scoped search with the appropriate bind. Illustrative output: anonymous search is denied but a domain bind succeeds. Interpretation: continue authenticated domain mapping.
verify: Record DC, base DN, bind identity and actual returned attributes; RootDSE alone is not a complete directory dump.
failure: Stronger-auth-required may mean TLS/signing policy; invalid credentials or an empty base require different fixes.

recognition.where: Identify the directory endpoint and query RootDSE before a subtree search under a known bind identity.
recognition.spot: RootDSE supplies the search base; it does not grant arbitrary anonymous subtree access.
recognition.confirm: Check bind identity, transport/signing requirements and read visibility on the selected objects.
recognition.enabled: A correctly authenticated scoped search returns expected objects: continue domain mapping.
recognition.ruledout: Anonymous subtree search is denied: reject anonymous enumeration while retaining a known-authenticated option.

procedure:
> **Recognition:** LDAP commonly appears on TCP/389 or TCP/636; Global Catalog on TCP/3268 or 3269; Kerberos on TCP/UDP 88. Applications may listen elsewhere, so follow protocol evidence rather than port labels. ##### Baseline: discover naming contexts > **Prerequisite:** LDAP reachability. **Coverage:** RootDSE only; this can work even when directory searches require authentication. **Decisive output:** `defaultNamingContext` and `dnsHostName`. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://TARGET:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext configurationNamingContext dnsHostName ``` Convert `DC=corp,DC=example` into `corp.example` for DNS/Kerberos work. Preserve the server's exact hostname because Kerberos is name-sensitive.
LDAPS and certificate-name inspection ```bash openssl s_client -connect TARGET:636 -servername DC_HOST A certificate can disclose domain/DC names. A TLS validation error is a client trust/name issue, not proof that LDAP is unavailable.
##### Anonymous directory search > **Prerequisite:** known base DN and server permitting anonymous search. **Failure cue:** `Inappropriate authentication` or `Insufficient access` closes only the anonymous path. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description ``` ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectClass=group)' cn member description ``` ##### Authenticated search > **Prerequisite:** a valid directory identity. **Decisive output:** objects/attributes unavailable anonymously. Avoid placing a real password in shell history when an interactive prompt is available. ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 \ -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName userAccountControl ```
Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately ```bash ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=computer)' \ dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=group)' cn member ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf ```
##### Kerberos prerequisites before an attack Kerberos failures are often name/time/route failures rather than credential failures. Establish: ```bash getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u nmap -Pn -sV -p 88,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 DC_IP -oN dc-services.txt ``` > **Interpretation:** resolve `DOMAIN` and `DC_HOST` consistently, keep clock skew within Kerberos tolerance, and ensure the KDC is reached through the selected route. `KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN` points to identity/domain naming; `KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW` points to time; `KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED` normally points to authentication material. ##### Handoff - New users, groups, computers, SPNs or domain names → [domain mapping](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/01-domain-mapping.md). - A user confirmed without preauthentication → [Kerberos and identity transitions](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/03-kerberos-and-identity-transitions.md). - Valid credentials → rerun authenticated LDAP plus SMB/share/remote-access enumeration. - Certificate templates/AD CS clues → [AD CS and object-control abuse](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/06-ad-lateral-movement/04-object-control-adcs-and-domain-compromise.md).
